## **Previously on 201**
### **Phrase Structure Rules (PSRs) for VP, TP**
<br><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:#CC0033">VP</span></b> → (AdvP+) <b><span style="color:#CC0033">V</span></b> (NP) (NP) (AdvP+) (PP+) (AdvP+)</h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:brown">TP</span></b> → NP <b><span style="color:brown">(T)</span> VP</b></h3><br><br>
- <h3><b><i>Arthur thoughtfully ate a bowl of hot oatmeal for breakfast.</i></b></h3><br><br>
- <h3><b>steps of drawing <span style="color:#CC0033">trees</span> for simple sentences</b></h3>

---
## **Steps for Drawing Trees**
<br>
1. write the sentence at the bottom of the page – leave yourself **plenty of room**<br><br>
2. label the **part of speech** of each word<br><br>
3. sentences have a subject <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span> and predicate **VP** – try to identify these first, and draw the subject<br><br>
4. trees should ALWAYS follow **PSR**s, so try to identify elements that can be part of rules for different phrases<br><br>
5. every <span style="color:blue"><b>noun</b></span>, <span style="color:orange"><b>adjective</b></span>, <span style="color:deeppink"><b>adverb</b></span>, <span style="color:green"><b>preposition</b></span> has its own corresponding phrase <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span>, <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span>, <span style="color:deeppink"><b>AdvP</b></span>, <span style="color:green"><b>PP</b></span><br><br>
6. smaller trees first, then figure out how they connect to the rest of the tree<br><br>
<b>some notes</b>
- VPs can have lots of elements, so figure them out last
- **pay attention to what modifies what** – any phrase that modifies a word should be its **sibling**
- because of the way English is structured, it can often be easier to start at the end and work **backwards**

## **Simple and Complex Sentences**
<br>
.pull-left[
- so far we've been studying **simple sentences: sentences** with **one** subject <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span> and one predicate <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>VP</b></span><br><br>
- now we're going to talk about **complex sentences** : sentencesthat have another sentence (clause) **embedded** inside of them<br><br>
  - *She said [that <b><span style="color:blue">she went to China</span></b>]*.<br><br>
  - *I bought an umbrella [because<b><span style="color:blue"> it was raining</span></b>]*.<br><br>
  - *That's the movie [<b><span style="color:blue">I saw</span></b>]*.<br><br>
  - *The book [that <b><span style="color:blue">I read</span></b>] was very interesting*.
]

</div>
]

.pull-left[
## **Complex Sentences**
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/1007/shechina1.png" width="100%">
]
.pull-right[
<br><br>
- A **complementiser** can connect two <b><span style="color:brown">TP</span></b>s together<br><br>
- **two parts** of a complex sentence:<br><br>
- <b><span style="color:blue">dependent clause</span></b> (aka subordinate clause, embedded clause, embedded sentence) – the sentence that has been **inserted** into the larger sentence<br><br>
  - *She said [that <b><span style="color:blue"> she went to China</span></b>]*.<br><br>
- <b><span style="color:green">main clause</span></b> (aka independent clause, main sentence) – the **full** sentence, technically **including the dependent clause**, since the dependent clause is inside of the main clause<br><br>
  - *<b><span style="color:green">She said [that she went to China]</span></b>*.
]

---
## **Complementisers**
<br>
- dependent clauses are usually linked to main clauses with a special type of word called a **complementiser** or **subordinating conjunction** (relative pronouns are a subtype):<br><br>
  - *that*, *which*, *because*, *if*, *so*, *since*, *which*, *who*, *although*, *where*...<br><br>
  - *She said <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>CP</sub></span> <b><span style="color:blue">that</span></b> she went to China <span style="color:deeppink">]</span> *.<br><br>
  - *I bought an umbrella <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>CP</sub></span>  <b><span style="color:blue">because</span></b> it was raining <span style="color:deeppink">]</span>*.<br><br>
  - *Please tell me <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>CP</sub></span>  <b><span style="color:blue">if</span></b> you're going to the store <span style="color:deeppink">]</span>*.<br><br>
- sometimes the complementiser is **omitted** (often in English, that can be variably omitted):<br><br>
  - *She said <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>CP</sub></span>  <b><span style="color:blue">(that)</span></b> she went to China <span style="color:deeppink">]</span>*.<br><br>
  - *The book <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>CP</sub></span>  <b><span style="color:blue">(that)</span></b> I read<span style="color:deeppink">]</span> is about dinosaurs*.<br><br>
  - *Ben thought <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>CP</sub></span>  <b><span style="color:blue">(that)</span></b> he was going to be late<span style="color:deeppink">]</span>*.

---
## **Structure of Dependent Clauses**
<br>
.pull-left[
- dependent clauses are **embedded sentences**, so we will also take them as a <span style="color:brown"><b>TP</b></span> <br><br>
- dependent clause <span style="color:brown"><b>TP</b></span>s are then inserted into a larger constituent called the **complementizer phrase** or <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></span>: <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></span> → **(C)** <span style="color:brown"><b>TP</b></span>
  - C (complementizer), is optional<br><br>
- <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></span> is then inserted into the **main clause**<br><br>
- **note** that some dependent clauses don NOT have an explicit subject NP <br><br>
  - *He wants <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>TP</sub></span> <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>Ø</b></span> to go to Machu Picchu <span style="color:deeppink">]</span>*.<br><br>
  - *I know the author <span style="color:green">[<sub>CP</sub></span> who <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>TP</sub></span> <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>Ø</b></span> wrote this book <span style="color:deeppink">]</span> <span style="color:green">]</span>*.
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/1007/shechina.png" width="50%">
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/1007/wrotebook.png" width="65%">
</div>
]

## **CPs inside VPs**
<br>
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/1007/merlinasked.png" width="60%">
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/1007/because3.png" width="60%">
</div>
]
.pull-right[
- four roles <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></span> can play in a sentence: <br><br>
1. take the role of an <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span>, acting as the **object** <br><br>
  - *Merlin <span style="color:#CC0033">[<sub>VP</sub></span> asked <span style="color:blue">[<sub>NP</sub></span> a question <span style="color:blue">]</sub></span> <span style="color:#CC0033">]</sub></span>*.
  - → *Merlin <span style="color:#CC0033">[<sub>VP</sub></span> asked <span style="color:teal">[<sub>CP</sub></span></sub> where I went <span style="color:teal">]</sub></span> <span style="color:#CC0033">]</sub></span>*.<br><br>
2. take the role of <span style="color:deeppink"><b>AdvP</b></span>, acting as an **adjunct**<br><br>
  - *I was <span style="color:#CC0033">[<sub>VP</sub></span> running <span style="color:deeppink">[<sub>AdvP</sub></span> quickly <span style="color:deeppink">]</sub></span> <span style="color:#CC0033">]</sub></span>*.
  - → *I was <span style="color:#CC0033">[<sub>VP</sub></span> running <span style="color:teal">[<sub>CP</sub></span> because I missed the bus <span style="color:teal">]</sub></span> <span style="color:#CC0033">]</sub></span>*.<br><br>
  
- since these <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></sub></span>s go inside **VP**s, let's modify our **VP** rule to account for these two cases:<br>
  - **VP** → (AdvP+) **V** (NP) **({**<span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></sub></span>, <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></sub></span>**})** (AdvP+) (PP+) (AdvP+) <span style="color:teal"><b>(CP+)</b></sub></span>
]

---
## **CPs inside NPs**
<br>
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/1007/girl.png" width="80%">
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/1007/girlimet.png" width="100%">
</div>
]
.pull-right[
- four roles <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></span> can play in a sentence: <br><br>
- act **like** an <span style="color:orange"><b>AdjP</b></span>, modifying a noun and going inside an <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span><br><br>
  - *<span style="color:blue">[<sub>NP</sub></span> The girl <span style="color:blue">]</sub></span> studies linguistics*.
  - *<span style="color:blue">[<sub>NP</sub></span> The girl <span style="color:teal">[<sub>CP</sub></span> that I met <span style="color:teal">]</span> <span style="color:blue">]</span> studies linguistics*.<br><br>
- these can go inside an <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></span> anywhere in the sentence:<br><br>
  - *<span style="color:blue">[<sub>NP</sub></span> The book <span style="color:teal">[<sub>CP</sub></span> I read <span style="color:teal">]</span> <span style="color:blue">]</span> is about geology*.
  - *She bought <span style="color:blue">[<sub>NP</sub></span> the book <span style="color:teal">[<sub>CP</sub></span> I read <span style="color:teal">]</span> ]*.<br><br>
- since these <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></sub></span>s go inside <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></sub></span>s, let's modify our <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></sub></span> rule:
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></sub></span> → (D) (AdjP+) **N** (PP+) <span style="color:teal"><b>(CP+)</b></sub></span>
]

---
## **CPs as the Subject**
<br><br><br><br>
.pull-left[
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/1007/elders.png" width="100%">
]
.pull-right[
- four roles <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></span> can play in a sentence: <br><br>
- act as **the subject**, going into a <span style="color:brown"><b>TP</b></sub></span><br><br>
  - *<span style="color:brown">[<sub>TP</sub></span> <span style="color:blue">[<sub>NP</sub></span> That story <span style="color:blue">]</span> impressed me <span style="color:brown">]</span>*.
  - *<span style="color:brown">[<sub>TP</sub></span> <span style="color:teal">[<sub>CP</sub></span> That he helped the elders <span style="color:teal">]</span> impressed me <span style="color:brown">]</span>*.<br><br>
- since these <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></sub></span>s go inside <span style="color:brown"><b>TP</b></sub></span>ss, let's modify our <span style="color:teal"><b>TP</b></sub></span>s rule:
  - <span style="color:brown"><b>TP</b></sub></span>s → **{**<span style="color:blue"><b>NP</b></sub></span>, <span style="color:teal"><b>CP</b></sub></span>**}** **(T)** VP
]

---
## **Modified Phrase Structure Rules for English**
<br>
.pull-left[
- <h3><b><span style="color:blue">NP</span></b> → (D) (AdjP+) <b><span style="color:blue">N</span></b> (PP+) <span style="color:teal">(CP+)</span></h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:green">PP</span></b> → <b><span style="color:green">P</span></b> NP</h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:orange">AdjP</span></b> → (AdvP) <b><span style="color:orange">Adj</span></b></h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:deeppink">AdvP</span></b> → (AdvP) <b><span style="color:deeppink">Adv</span></b></h3><br>
]
.pull-right[
- <h3><b><span style="color:brown">TP</span></b> → **{**<span style="color:blue">NP</span>, <span style="color:teal">CP</span>**}** <b><span style="color:brown">(T)</span></b> VP</h3><br>
- <h3><b><span style="color:teal">CP</span></b> → <b><span style="color:teal">(C)</span></b> TP</h3><br>
]
- <h3><b><span style="color:#CC0033">VP</span></b> → (AdvP+) <b><span style="color:#CC0033">V</span></b> (NP) (<span style="color:#CC0033">{</span><span style="color:blue">NP</span>, <span style="color:teal">CP</sub></span><span style="color:#CC0033">}</span>) (AdvP+) (PP+) (AdvP+) <span style="color:teal">(CP+)</span></h3>

---
## **Drawing Complex Sentences**
<br>
- if a sentence has **two main verbs** joined by a **complementizer**, it's **complex**<br><br>
- this doesn't include sentences with two main verbs joined by a **coordinating
conjunction** like <i><u>and</u></i>, <i><u>or</u></i>, <i><u>but</u></i><br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<i>I read a book **and** I took a walk</i>.
</div>
<br><br>
- then identify which of these verbs is in the **main** clause, and which is in the **subordinate** clause<br><br>
  - the **subordinate** clause is the one that <b><span style="color:blue">starts with a complementiser</span></b>
  - but be aware that the complementiser that is sometimes **omitted**
  - draw the tree for the subordinate clause first<br><br>
- draw the tree for the **main** clause without the subordinate clause, then figure out <b><span style="color:blue">how the two are connected</span></b><br><br>
  - does the subordinate clause modify a noun (goes in to <b><span style="color:blue">NP</span></b>)
  - is it part of the main clause's VP (goes in to **VP**)
  - is is the subject (goes into <b><span style="color:brown">TP</span></b>)

### **Thai vs English**
<br>

1. Thai has **classifiers** (no English equivalent)<br><br>
2. demonstratives (**this / that**) follow the noun in Thai but precede it in English<br><br>
3. the **progressive** is expressed by a **separate** word in Thai and the verb does not change form
]
